transcript.text: Bosch built-in microwave BFL524MS0B randomly stops part way through cooking, time still on the display. Opening and closing the door lets it carry on. Maybe once every few days.

## Most likely cause: the door interlock switches or latch

Your symptoms point to the door safety (interlock) switches or the door latch. When the oven briefly loses the "door closed" signal, it pauses the program exactly as if you'd opened the door. That's why the remaining time stays on the display and opening and closing the door resumes it.

Common reasons:
• A worn or weak microswitch. There are usually two or three behind the latch, and one can start making poor contact.
• The door not seating fully. Worn hinges, a slightly dropped door, or a cabinet that has shifted can leave the latch hooks only just engaging the switches.
• Dirt or grease on the latch hooks or around the latch slots in the frame.

A power blip would normally reset the display, and an overheat cut-out usually wouldn't clear just by opening the door. Neither fits as well.

## Things you can safely check yourself

1. Watch how the door closes. It should click shut cleanly without pushing. Check that the gap around it is even and the door doesn't sag on the latch side.
2. Clean the latch area. With the oven unplugged or isolated, wipe the latch hooks on the door and the slots in the frame. Remove any food or grease buildup.
3. Run a simple test. Heat a cup of water. While it runs, press gently on the door near the latch, then pull lightly on the handle without opening it. If the oven pauses, you've confirmed a door, latch, or switch problem.
4. Check that it's still flush in the cabinet. Make sure nothing is pressing on the door or frame, such as a cabinet door, trim, or handle.

## Leave the inside to a professional

The interlock switches are inside the casing. A microwave holds lethal voltages, even unplugged, because of its high-voltage capacitor. These switches are also what stop the oven running with the door open. Replacing them, adjusting the latch, or re-hanging the door is a job for a qualified technician, and on a built-in model the unit also has to come out of the housing.

• If it's under warranty (Bosch normally offers 2 years, sometimes more if registered), contact Bosch service. Describe it as "stops mid-cycle as if the door has been opened; resumes after reopening the door."
• If it's out of warranty, a Bosch engineer or an independent appliance repairer can usually fix this fairly cheaply. Switches and latches are inexpensive parts.

It's not dangerous as it is, because the fault makes the oven stop, not run with the door open. But it tends to get more frequent, so it's worth sorting before it becomes unusable.

I've checked a few of those. There was some grease around the door hooks and latch slots, which I cleaned, but it has still happened once since. It seems to happen more when I close the door gently. The door might sit very slightly lower on the handle side, but I can't be sure. There's no smell, sparks or tripping, and I can't take it out of the housing because it's screwed into the tall unit. It's out of Bosch's 2-year warranty, but I'd pay for a Bosch engineer. Does that pattern point to the switch or the door alignment?

## It points to marginal latch engagement, most likely made worse by the door alignment

The "happens more when I close it gently" detail is the key clue. When you close the door gently, the latch hooks travel only just far enough to press the switches, so any small vibration or a slight shift during cooking can break contact and pause the program. A firmer close pushes the hooks further in and holds them there.

That can come from either cause:
• Door alignment. If the door has dropped slightly on the handle side, the hooks sit lower or shallower in the slots and only just reach the switch plungers. Your possible sag fits this.
• A worn switch. A tired microswitch needs more travel or pressure before it makes reliable contact, so a gentle close isn't quite enough.

In practice these often go together. A slightly sagging door puts uneven strain on the switches over time, and an engineer will usually check both, possibly replacing a switch and correcting the door or hinges in the same visit.

## Two quick checks before the engineer comes

1. Compare the gaps. Look at the gap between the door and the frame or tall unit along the top and bottom edges. If it's wider at one corner on the handle side, or the door edge isn't parallel with the cabinet line, the door has dropped.
2. Lift test. While heating a cup of water, gently lift the handle upwards a millimetre or two without pulling it open, then press it down slightly. If pressing down (or letting it sag) pauses it but lifting doesn't, alignment is the stronger suspect. If light pressure in any direction pauses it, a weak switch is more likely.

Don't force anything, and stop if the door feels loose.

## Booking the Bosch engineer

Booking through Bosch is a good route, especially since the unit is fixed into the tall housing and they'll be used to removing it. When you book, mention:
• The pattern: it pauses mid-cycle, the time stays on the display, and reopening and closing the door resumes it.
• That it happens more after a gentle close.
• The possible slight drop on the handle side.

That points them straight at the interlock switches, latch and hinges, so they're more likely to arrive with the right parts. Ask about a fixed-price repair, which Bosch often offers for out-of-warranty appliances. It's also worth asking whether they'll consider a goodwill contribution given the oven's age, since a door or switch fault shortly after the warranty ends is arguably earlier than you'd reasonably expect.

## Safety note

Keep using it for now, since pausing is the safety system working. But stop using it and isolate it straight away if it ever runs with the door open, keeps running after you open the door, or the door won't latch at all.
